questions.prompt: What is the chapter's main implementation claim?
choices: A good checklist works perfectly the first time if the idea is correct
The first practical checklist attempt reveals friction that has to be revised
Resistance mainly proves professionals should be overruled quickly

explanation.gentle: The chapter says the first try matters because it exposes what has to be improved.
explanation.direct: Gawande treats first-version friction as part of building a usable checklist, not as proof against the idea.
explanation.competitive: The first draft is a stress test, not a final verdict.

questions.prompt: Why does the early WHO pilot matter in this chapter?
choices: It provides the first real setting where the checklist idea meets practice
It proves the final checklist was already complete on day one
It shows that design work no longer matters once a pilot begins

explanation.gentle: The pilot is where the abstract idea first gets tested in real use.
explanation.direct: The chapter needs the pilot because theory alone cannot show where a checklist will feel awkward or workable.
explanation.competitive: The room exposes what the whiteboard could not.

choices: Only that professionals dislike being told what to do
That the checklist may be too long, mistimed, or out of rhythm with the work
That checklists should always be abandoned quickly

explanation.gentle: Pushback can show real design friction.
explanation.direct: The chapter says resistance may reflect usability problems rather than empty pride alone.
explanation.competitive: Sometimes the room is spotting the flaw, not dodging the standard.

questions.prompt: A team says a new checklist interrupts the work at the wrong moment. What Chapter 5 response fits best?
choices: Keep the checklist unchanged to prove authority
Treat the complaint as feedback about timing and revise the checklist's use point
Drop the checklist because any friction means the idea failed

explanation.gentle: The chapter says implementation problems can be repaired through revision.
explanation.direct: Bad timing is exactly the kind of friction the first try is supposed to expose.
explanation.competitive: Fix the rhythm before you judge the tool.

questions.prompt: Why is it wrong to treat the first awkward version as proof that the checklist idea failed?
choices: Because early drafts are expected to reveal what real use demands
Because every first version should be obeyed no matter what
Because the chapter says usability never matters

explanation.gentle: The first try is useful because it shows what needs improvement.
explanation.direct: The chapter distinguishes idea failure from first-version friction.
explanation.competitive: A clumsy draft is data, not defeat.

questions.prompt: What makes a checklist gain credibility in this chapter?
choices: High-status people ordering everyone to accept it
Revision that respects the workflow while keeping essential checks intact
Adding more steps so nobody can skip anything

explanation.gentle: Credibility grows when the tool becomes usable and still protects what matters.
explanation.direct: The chapter ties trust to practical fit plus preserved purpose, not to hierarchy alone.
explanation.competitive: The tool earns belief when it survives the room without losing its teeth.

questions.prompt: A family packing checklist feels clumsy on the first trip. What Chapter 5 lesson applies?
choices: The checklist should be thrown out because first use felt awkward
The checklist should be revised so the key pause stays but the sequence fits real use better
The family should memorize everything and stop using lists

explanation.gentle: The chapter says revision is part of making a checklist usable.
explanation.direct: You keep the checklist's purpose while improving its timing or shape.
explanation.competitive: Sharpen the tool instead of sulking over version one.

questions.prompt: What is the danger if a team trims every uncomfortable step just to reduce resistance?
choices: The checklist may lose the disciplined pause that made it useful
The checklist will automatically become more credible
The chapter says discomfort is always irrelevant

explanation.gentle: A checklist can become too weak if revision removes its essential check.
explanation.direct: The chapter's balance is usability without surrendering the purpose of the pause.
explanation.competitive: If you sand off every hard edge, you may erase the point.

questions.prompt: What is the chapter's deepest implementation lesson?
choices: Good ideas should wait for perfect acceptance before testing
Implementation is where design becomes real through iterative refinement
Professional resistance is mostly a distraction from technical correctness

explanation.gentle: The chapter says the real checklist is built through testing and revision.
explanation.direct: Implementation is not separate from design. It is the place where design gets corrected by reality.
explanation.competitive: The room finishes what the theory starts.

questions.prompt: What question does the chapter hand to the next chapter?
choices: How to prove one early pilot already settled the whole argument
How good checklist builders learn to make lists shorter, sharper, and more usable
Why all resistance disappears once a checklist is announced

explanation.gentle: The next chapter asks what good checklist design actually requires.
explanation.direct: Once the first try exposes friction, the book moves toward design discipline and construction rules.
explanation.competitive: The next fight is building a tool the room can live with.
